Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either increase investment or boost domestic consumption. With the marginal returns on traditional infrastructure and real estate investment severely diminished, the only sustainable path is to increase household consumption. This requires profound structural reform. The ultimate goal of such reform is to transfer wealth and income share from the state and corporate sectors to households."

This is increasingly becoming how most Chinese economists understand the Chinese economy, although only recently have they been so public about it. The key point here (and one with which many Chinese economists still disagree) is that with marginal returns on most investment so low, reducing China's trade surplus through an increase in investment will only make the longer-term adjustment worse.

China, in other words, should be reducing investment, not raising it, in order to regain control over misallocated capital and surging debt, but this also means that the only way to rebalance domestically and reduce the trade surplus requires that saving declines even faster.

Li Wei lists one of the ways the saving share of GDP can decline, by transferring income share from the state and corporate sectors to households in order to boost consumption growth relative to the growth in production.

He is right, of course. This is certainly one way to reduce saving and bring the trade surplus down, but it won't be easy because doing so will undermine China's manufacturing competitiveness. 

Unfortunately, there is only one other alternative, and it is much worse. The reduction in saving can also occur with a sharp fall in production growth.  As production declines faster that consumption, the saving share automatically declines.

Historically this has been how most countries with a similar problem have been forced to adjust, mainly because, like China, they postponed boosting consumption growth for far too long and instead doubled down on their high-investment-growth model. 

Beijing, of course, will want to do everything it can to avoid this form of adjustment, but the longer it postpones adjustment by boosting consumption growth, the more likely the Chinese economy will adjust through a fall in production growth.

Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China."

What Xinhua chose not to mention in its article, but what nearly everyone else will focus on, is that Chinese banks recorded a net decline of 340 billion yuan in new yuan loans in July, well below already-low expectations for a 120-130 billion increase.

But while the sharp and unexpected decline in lending in July will get most of the attention from analysts and the press, what is much more important to me is that total social financing, the best proxy for total debt, actually grew quite strongly in July, by 1.4 trillion yuan.

This highlights what we have been seeing all year, which is that China's financing activity is undergoing a structural shift, with the economy relying more than ever on state-led borrowing – and less than ever on private-sector borrowing – to support growth.

A few thoughts on today’s SemiAnalysis TPU report.

1. I am deeply disappointed with the way SemiAnalysis continues to report on these issues. I have raised the same concern before with Micron, CPO delays, SOCAMM, and 8 high HBM4. I do not think they simply fabricate stories out of thin air. The problem is how they communicate them. They often seem too quick to report information that has not yet been confirmed, and even when the underlying facts are directionally correct, the ambiguity in the wording and framing repeatedly creates major misunderstandings in the market.

2. This TPU report is another example. If you actually read the substance, the 2026 AVGO TPU downward revision is explicitly attributed to supply constraints and challenges ramping CoWoS S. The 2027 revision is attributed to greater Broadcom capacity allocation toward other customers such as Meta and OpenAI. The AMD discussion, meanwhile, is about a potential TPU v10 project.

The report does not establish any causal relationship between these two issues. Yet by placing them directly next to each other, it created a framing that could very easily be interpreted by institutional and professional investors quickly scanning the report as a simple 

"AMD Long, AVGO Short narrative"

I am not saying that SemiAnalysis intentionally framed it this way. However, if they did not anticipate that kind of market interpretation, then I think this reflects a serious communication and editorial problem. On the other hand, if they did anticipate it, then I have to ask why they did not include even a single clear sentence explaining that the AVGO TPU downward revision was not being attributed to AMD.

3. Anyone who understands the ASIC business even at a basic level should know how dangerous this kind of overinterpretation can be. AVGO signed a long term agreement with Google just this April to develop and supply future generations of TPUs. The claim that AMD is already taking Broadcom’s TPU volume is simply not supported by the information presented in this report.

And if the AMD collaboration they are referring to is related to on package CPU cores, then that is not really a threatening area for AVGO in the first place, because Broadcom is not competing in the x86 CPU market. A much simpler interpretation would be that Google may need x86 cores for specific use cases, such as RL workloads, and AMD could be relevant there.

4. Today I spoke not only with people in the semiconductor industry, but also with a friend who works at a New York hedge fund. He agreed with my view completely, while also pointing out that we cannot ignore either the influence of SemiAnalysis reports or the direction in which capital ultimately moves.

Is this really healthy market behavior? This is the part that concerns me most.

I assume SemiAnalysis understands very well how much influence its reports can have on the market. If so, I believe that influence should come with a much greater degree of care in how information is framed and communicated. This is not the first time this year that I have had concerns about this type of reporting, which is why I felt it was important to call it out directly this time.

5. In the end, I believe the ASIC business comes down to the quality of the IP and the ability to secure sufficient manufacturing capacity. AVGO has competed with Marvell on these fronts for many years and has continued to survive and win. It will continue to face challenges from other competitors on these same fronts, whether that competitor is AMD, Marvell, or someone else.

So let us think again about what we should actually be asking.

Why did AVGO recently enter into such a large strategic MOU with Samsung?

What is AVGO preparing for next in its ASIC business?

From a technical perspective, what are the actual risks facing its ASIC business?

From AVGO’s perspective, in what ways could a more diversified customer base actually become a long term positive?

I believe these are the questions that deserve much deeper analysis.

Why does SemiAnalysis not address them?

I am genuinely disappointed with this report. At this point, I am honestly irritated that I keep having to spend my valuable time rechecking the same facts every time this kind of ambiguous reporting creates another round of confusion in the market.

Finally wrapping up five weeks in China. I spent most of my time in Beijing and Shanghai, with detours to Hangzhou, Suzhou. I got some time with my husband and toddler, but most of the trip was work: deepening relationships and getting much more up to speed on what’s happening on the ground.

There’s a pretty palpable shift in the industries we cover. Things are busier, there’s a lot more activity, and it really feels like things are heating up. I’m not saying that will necessarily show up in financial performance immediately, but the mood is noticeably different from a year ago.

I can’t say too much more because all of our @techbuzzchina trips are now private, and I won’t be sharing detailed information about participants or itineraries. But we continue to put together bespoke trips, and everyone we’ve taken to China has wanted to bring another group back. At this point, most of our business comes through referrals and word of mouth, and there are plenty of past clients you can talk to about what we’ve been able to do for them.

I really do think China is one of those places where, at least in frontier technology, you need to be on the ground every few months to understand what’s actually happening. I say that as someone who is on calls with China pretty much every night when I’m back in the U.S. Even so, being here is completely different.

We’ve continued expanding our network across new cities and verticals, and I’m leaving with an absurd amount of interesting new information, even if much of it can’t be written about because these conversations are off the record.

Mostly, I’m just incredibly excited about this space. It’s hard to imagine a more intellectually stimulating time to be covering China tech. We have a bunch of new projects in the works, several new partners signed up, and a lot more coming.

Bye for now!!
